title: IELTS Academic Reading Practice Test 42
instructions: You should spend about 20 minutes on each passage. Answer all questions.

passages.title: Gardens with a Purpose
passages.text:
A. The botanical garden began as a teaching collection attached to a medical faculty. Physicians needed to recognise the plants their remedies were made from, misidentification was a serious hazard, and a garden of labelled specimens was the only reliable way to teach the difference between a useful plant and a similar dangerous one. The ornamental garden and the scientific one have quite separate ancestries.

B. Long-distance plant transfer changed the institution's purpose entirely. Once ships could carry living material between continents, gardens became the nodes of a network moving crops from where they grew to where they might be grown profitably, and the botanical garden of an imperial power was an instrument of economic policy. Rubber, tea, cinchona and coffee were all moved deliberately in this way, and the modern agricultural geography of several countries is a direct result.

C. The technical obstacle was keeping plants alive on a voyage. Salt spray, darkness below deck, insufficient fresh water and voyages of many months killed the great majority of material shipped, and survival rates before the middle of the nineteenth century were dismal. A sealed glazed case that recycled its own moisture and admitted light transformed those rates, and this single unremarkable object is responsible for much of what grows commercially where it does.

D. The gardens' role has been substantially reversed within the last century. An institution built to distribute plants around the world now works largely to prevent unintended distribution, since introduced species without their natural controls are among the principal causes of extinction on islands and in freshwater systems. The same expertise in moving and establishing plants is now applied to identifying and containing them.

E. Conservation collections carry a limitation that is rarely stated to visitors. A species held as a few individuals in cultivation is preserved as a specimen and not as a population: it loses genetic diversity with every generation, adapts to garden conditions rather than wild ones, and cannot easily be returned to a habitat that no longer exists. Living collections buy time and do not substitute for the place a plant came from.

F. What these institutions hold that is least visible may be the most valuable. Pressed and dried specimens, some centuries old, record what grew where and when in a form no other source provides, and they have been used to establish shifts in flowering time, changes in range and the composition of vanished habitats. A collection assembled to answer questions about identification is answering questions its collectors could not have posed.

passages.title: The Tissue That Flows
passages.text:
Blood is best understood as an organ rather than a fluid, and transfusion as a transplant rather than a top-up. It carries oxygen, distributes heat, transports signalling molecules, delivers the immune system to where it is needed, and clots on demand — a combination of functions that no single manufactured substitute has matched, which is why decades of work on artificial blood have produced useful partial solutions and nothing that replaces it.

Early transfusion failed catastrophically and unpredictably, and the reason was not understood for centuries. Some recipients recovered and others died rapidly, with no pattern anyone could identify, and the practice was abandoned and revived repeatedly. The explanation was the existence of blood groups: molecules on the surface of red cells that the recipient's immune system either recognises or attacks, so compatibility is a property of the pair rather than of either person.

Storage is the constraint that shapes every blood service. Red cells can be kept for a matter of weeks under refrigeration and platelets for a few days at room temperature, which means supply cannot be built up in advance of demand and must be continuously replenished. A service therefore depends on a steady flow of donors rather than on a stock, and its planning problem resembles that of a fresh food supply chain more than that of a pharmacy.

The safety of the supply was transformed by events that also destroyed public confidence. Transmission of infection through transfusion, and the slow institutional response to early evidence of it, caused a great deal of harm and produced the modern apparatus of donor screening, testing and traceability. The current supply in high-income countries is safer than at any previous point by a wide margin, and the caution that produced this is a direct inheritance from the period when it was not.

Whether to pay donors is a question where the evidence has moved. Paying was long held to reduce safety by attracting donors who would conceal disqualifying information, an argument formed when testing was poor and the concealment mattered enormously; with modern testing, the safety difference has narrowed considerably, and the remaining arguments are about supply stability, equity and what a society wishes to treat as a commodity. Different countries have settled this differently for defensible reasons.

The clinical direction of travel is towards transfusing less. Trials comparing liberal with restrictive transfusion thresholds have repeatedly found that giving less blood produces outcomes as good or better in most situations, and that the intuition to correct a number is not the same as treating a patient. Programmes built on this reduce transfusions substantially with no measurable harm, which is a rare instance of a treatment being improved by being withheld.

passages.title: Selling the Second Hour
passages.text:
The video game business has passed through three economic models in four decades, and each transition changed what was made rather than merely how it was sold. A product sold once in a box rewards a finished experience that justifies its price at the moment of purchase; a product sold as ongoing access rewards retention; a product given away and monetised afterwards rewards whatever brings a player back tomorrow. The design follows the revenue and always has.

Development economics push relentlessly towards concentration. Costs for the largest titles now rival those of major films, and the failure of one such project can end a studio, so publishers favour established properties with a demonstrated audience, and the sequel is a risk-management decision before it is a creative one. The proportion of large releases that are continuations of existing series has risen for exactly this reason.

Distribution changed the position of small developers more than any other factor. When physical retail controlled access to shelves, a small studio needed a publisher to reach anyone; digital storefronts removed that gatekeeper and made it possible for two people to reach a global audience. The gate did not disappear, however — it moved to discovery, and being findable among many thousands of releases is now the scarce resource that shelf space used to be.

Free distribution with later payment is where the ethical questions concentrate. A game that costs nothing to start and sells advantages, cosmetics or time savings afterwards derives a disproportionate share of its revenue from a small minority of heavy spenders, and design decisions that increase spending among that minority are not always decisions that improve the game for anyone. Where the mechanics resemble gambling, several jurisdictions have concluded that they should be regulated as such.

The labour pattern has been criticised for a long time and has proved persistent. Intense overtime before release is widespread, is a predictable consequence of estimating schedules for creative work that cannot be estimated accurately, and persists because a large supply of people who want to work in the industry accepts conditions that other software employers could not impose. It is an economic outcome rather than a cultural failing of the people managing it.

What the industry demonstrates most clearly is the power of what is measured. When a business can observe every action a player takes, it optimises for what it can see — session length, return rate, conversion — and those measures are proxies for enjoyment that diverge from it under pressure. A game optimised to be played is not the same as a game optimised to be enjoyed, and telling the difference requires exactly the judgement that the data was supposed to replace.
